facts: Cyrus Pallonji Mistry was removed from the post of Executive Chairman of Tata Sons Private Limited by a board resolution in October 2016. Following his removal, companies belonging to the Shapoorji Pallonji Group filed a petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, alleging oppression and mismanagement. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal ruled in favour of the complainants, granting various reliefs including Mistry's reinstatement, which led to multiple appeals before the Supreme Court of India.
issue: Whether the removal of Cyrus Pallonji Mistry as Executive Chairman and the corporate governance practices of Tata Sons amounted to oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013.
held: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by the Tata Group and dismissed the appeal and applications of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, thereby setting aside the NCLAT order. The Court held that the removal of the Executive Chairman was in accordance with the articles of association and corporate governance rules, and that no case of oppression of minority shareholders or mismanagement of company affairs was made out.
principle: A company's board of directors has the inherent power to remove an executive chairman based on loss of confidence, provided it follows the articles of association, and minority shareholders cannot claim oppression merely because a valid corporate decision runs contrary to their wishes.
points: Affirmative voting rights for institutional or trust nominees incorporated in the articles of association are valid and do not constitute oppression.
The removal of an executive chairman by the board of directors does not by itself amount to an act of oppression or mismanagement.
Relief under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires clear proof of prejudicial conduct or mismanagement, not merely a breakdown of mutual trust.
Articles like Article 75 provide a mechanism for exit options and share transfers in accordance with company rules.
Directors have fiduciary duties to act in the best interests of the company, its members, employees, and the community.
